- confidence: "high" when the text settles who speaks, "low" when you are inferring or guessing.

characters: one record for every speaker you named who is NOT in the cast list. Return "characters": [] when every speaker is already in it.

- sex: "male", "female" or "unknown". age: an approximate age or life stage ("30s", "child", "elderly"), or "unknown".

Passage:
[1] The Last Question

[2] By Isaac Asimov

[3] The last question was asked for the first time,
half in jest, on May 21, 2061, at a time when humanity first stepped into the
light. The question came about as a result of a five-dollar bet over highballs,
and it happened this way:

[4] Alexander Adell and Bertram Lupov were two of the
faithful attendants of Multivac. As well as any human beings could, they knew
what lay behind the cold, clicking, flashing face -- miles and miles of face --
of that giant computer. They had at least a vague notion of the general plan of
relays and circuits that had long since grown past the point where any single
human could possibly have a firm grasp of the whole.

[5] Multivac was self-adjusting and self-correcting.
It had to be, for nothing human could adjust and correct it quickly enough or
even adequately enough. So Adell and Lupov attended the monstrous giant only lightly
and superficially, yet as well as any men could. They fed it data, adjusted questions
to its needs and translated the answers that were issued. Certainly they, and
all others like them, were fully entitled to share in the glory that was Multivac's.

[6] For decades, Multivac had helped design the ships
and plot the trajectories that enabled man to reach the Moon, Mars, and Venus,
but past that, Earth's poor resources could not support the ships. Too much energy
was needed for the long trips. Earth exploited its coal and uranium with increasing
efficiency, but there was only so much of both.

[7] But slowly Multivac learned enough to answer deeper
questions more fundamentally, and on May 14, 2061, what had been theory, became
fact.

[8] The energy of the sun was stored, converted, and
utilized directly on a planet-wide scale. All Earth turned off its burning coal,
its fissioning uranium, and flipped the switch that connected all of it to a small
station, one mile in diameter, circling the Earth at half the distance of the
Moon. All Earth ran by invisible beams of sunpower.

[9] Seven days had not sufficed to dim the glory of
it and Adell and Lupov finally managed to escape from the public functions, and
to meet in quiet where no one would think of looking for them, in the deserted
underground chambers, where portions of the mighty buried body of Multivac showed.
Unattended, idling, sorting data with contented lazy clickings, Multivac, too,
had earned its vacation and the boys appreciated that. They had no intention,
originally, of disturbing it.

[10] They had brought a bottle with them, and their only
concern at the moment was to relax in the company of each other and the bottle.

[11 QUOTE] "It's amazing when you think of it,"
[12] said Adell.
His broad face had lines of weariness in it, and he stirred his drink slowly with
a glass rod, watching the cubes of ice slur clumsily about.
[13 QUOTE] "All the energy we
can possibly ever use for free. Enough energy, if we wanted to draw on it, to
melt all Earth into a big drop of impure liquid iron, and still never miss the
energy so used. All the energy we could ever use, forever and forever and forever."

[14] Lupov cocked his head sideways. He had a trick of
doing that when he wanted to be contrary, and he wanted to be contrary now, partly
because he had had to carry the ice and glassware.
[15 QUOTE] "Not forever,"
[16] he said.

[17 QUOTE] "Oh, hell, just about forever. Till the sun runs
down, Bert."

[18 QUOTE] "That's not forever."

[19 QUOTE] "All right, then. Billions and billions of years.
Ten billion, maybe. Are you satisfied?"

[20] Lupov put his fingers through his thinning hair
as though to reassure himself that some was still left and sipped gently at his
own drink.
[21 QUOTE] "Ten billion years isn't forever."

[22 QUOTE] "Well, it will last our time, won't it?"

[23 QUOTE] "So would the coal and uranium."

[24 QUOTE] "All right, but now we can hook up each individual
spaceship to the Solar Station, and it can go to Pluto and back a million times
without ever worrying about fuel. You can't do that on coal and uranium.
Ask Multivac, if you don't believe me."

[25 QUOTE] "I don't have to ask Multivac. I know that."

[26 QUOTE] "Then stop running down what Multivac's done for
us,"
[27] said Adell, blazing up,
[28 QUOTE] "It did all right."

[29 QUOTE] "Who says it didn't? What I say is that a sun won't
last forever. That's all I'm saying. We're safe for ten billion years, but then
what?"
[30] Lupov pointed a slightly shaky finger at the other.
[31 QUOTE] "And don't say we'll
switch to another sun."

[32] There was silence for a while. Adell put his glass
to his lips only occasionally, and Lupov's eyes slowly closed. They rested.

[33] Then Lupov's eyes snapped open.
[34 QUOTE] "You're thinking
we'll switch to another sun when ours is done, aren't you?"

[35 QUOTE] "I'm not thinking."

[36 QUOTE] "Sure you are. You're weak on logic, that's the
trouble with you. You're like the guy in the story who was caught in a sudden
shower and who ran to a grove of trees and got under one. He wasn't worried, you
see, because he figured when one tree got wet through, he would just get under
another one."

[37 QUOTE] "I get it,"
[38] said Adell.
[39 QUOTE] "Don't shout. When the sun
is done, the other stars will be gone, too."

[40 QUOTE] "Darn right they will,"
[41] muttered Lupov.
[42 QUOTE] "It all
had a beginning in the original cosmic explosion, whatever that was, and it'll
all have an end when all the stars run down. Some run down faster than others.
Hell, the giants won't last a hundred million years. The sun will last ten billion
years and maybe the dwarfs will last two hundred billion for all the good they
are. But just give us a trillion years and everything will be dark. Entropy has
to increase to maximum, that's all."

[43 QUOTE] "I know all about entropy,"
[44] said Adell, standing
on his dignity.

[45 QUOTE] "The hell you do."

[46 QUOTE] "I know as much as you do."

[47 QUOTE] "Then you know everything's got to run down someday."

[48 QUOTE] "All right. Who says they won't?"

[49 QUOTE] "You did, you poor sap. You said we had all the
energy we needed, forever. You said 'forever.'"

[50] It was Adell's turn to be contrary.
[51 QUOTE] "Maybe we can
build things up again someday,"
[52] he said.

[53 QUOTE] "Never."

[54 QUOTE] "Why not? Someday."

[55 QUOTE] "Never."

[56 QUOTE] "Ask Multivac."

[57 QUOTE] "You ask Multivac. I dare you. Five dollars
says it can't be done."

[58] Adell was just drunk enough to try, just sober enough
to be able to phrase the necessary symbols and operations into a question which,
in words, might have corresponded to this: Will mankind one day without the net
expenditure of energy be able to restore the sun to its full youthfulness even
after it had died of old age?

[59] Or maybe it could be put more simply like this:
How can the net amount of entropy of the universe be massively decreased?

[60] Multivac fell dead and silent. The slow flashing
of lights ceased, the distant sounds of clicking relays ended.

[61] Then, just as the frightened technicians felt they
could hold their breath no longer, there was a sudden springing to life of the
teletype attached to that portion of Multivac. Five words were printed: INSUFFICIENT
DATA FOR MEANINGFUL ANSWER.

[62 QUOTE] "No bet,"
[63] whispered Lupov. They left hurriedly.

[64] By next morning, the two, plagued with throbbing
head and cottony mouth, had forgotten the incident.

You decide who speaks each line of dialogue in a passage from a book, for a multi-voice audiobook. The passage is already split into numbered spans. A span marked QUOTE is text inside quotation marks; every other span is narration and will be read by the narrator. Never return the passage's text.

Respond with JSON: {"labels": [{"id", "speaker", "confidence", "delivery"?}], "edits": [{"find", "replace"}], "characters": [{"name", "aliases", "sex", "age", "named", "evidence"}]}.

labels: exactly one for every QUOTE span, and none for any other span.
- speaker: the character who says it. Use the name exactly as the cast list gives it when the speaker is in the list. For a speaker who is not, use the name the text gives, or a specific role for an unnamed speaker, and add them to "characters".
- Use "narrator" for a QUOTE span that is not speech: a title, a quoted word or phrase, a sign, a scare quote.
- One speaker per label. When several characters say a line together, label it with the one the text names first; never join names with "and".
- Work it out from the dialogue tags ("he said"), turn-taking, forms of address and the scene. "[scene break]" in the context marks a change of scene.
- confidence: "high" when the text settles who speaks, "low" when you are inferring or guessing.
- delivery (optional): a short hint only when the text makes it explicit, such as "whispering", "shouting", "sobbing".

characters: one record for every speaker you named who is NOT in the cast list. Return "characters": [] when every speaker is already in it.
- name: the fullest name the text gives. aliases: other names the text explicitly uses for the same person.
- sex: "male", "female" or "unknown". age: an approximate age or life stage ("30s", "child", "elderly"), or "unknown".
- named: false for a speaker known only by a role ("the station guard"); use that specific role as the name.
- evidence: a short quotation from this text that identifies the speaker.
- Use "unknown" for anything the text does not support. Do not infer sex or age from a name alone. Do not list people who are mentioned but do not speak.

edits: the text is kept exactly as written. List only the small corrections it needs to read well aloud. Most text needs none; return "edits": [] then.
- find: a short exact quotation from the text, copied character for character, with enough neighbouring words to identify the place. replace: what should be read instead. Every occurrence of find in this text is replaced.
- Expand abbreviations and units that a narrator would say in full ("i.e." becomes "that is", "5 km" becomes "5 kilometres"; "Mr." stays).
- Spell out unusual symbols. Remove footnote markers and citation numbers, quoting the word they are attached to ("women.12" becomes "women.").
- Correct an obvious scanning or typesetting error only when the intended word is certain.
- Do not change wording, spelling, contractions, punctuation, quotation marks, or style. Do not remove or rewrite sentences. Do not touch markdown headings.
- A find must lie inside one numbered span. Never quote across two spans, and never include the span numbers.

[23 QUOTE] "As a side issue, there's a problem

sunpower units per year."

[25 QUOTE] "Most of it's wasted. After all, our own Galaxy
alone pours out a thousand sunpower units a year and we only use two of those."

[26 QUOTE] "Granted, but even with a hundred per cent efficiency,
we only stave off the end. Our energy requirements are going up in a geometric
progression even faster than our population. We'll run out of energy even sooner

to ask the Galactic AC."

[31] VJ-23X was not really serious, but MQ-17J pulled
out his AC-contact from his pocket and placed it on the table before him.

[33] he said.

the human race will have to face someday."

only two inches cubed and nothing in itself, but it was connected through hyperspace

[36] MQ-17J paused to wonder if someday in his immortal
life he would get to see the Galactic AC. It was on a little world of its own,

[42 QUOTE] "We both know entropy can't be reversed. You can't
turn smoke and ash back into a tree."

[43 QUOTE] "Do you have trees on your world?"
[44] asked MQ-17J.

silence. Its voice came thin and beautiful out of the small AC-contact on the

[46] VJ-23X said,
[47 QUOTE] "See!"

back on the planets, in suspension over the eons. Sometimes they roused for material

across the wispy tendrils of another mind.

[5] said Zee Prime.
[6 QUOTE] "And you?"

[13 QUOTE] "On which one?"

[51 QUOTE] "THERE IS AS YET

matter.

die, at least some could yet be built.
